_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-07-06 08:28:21Z)**_

Great question — this is the real one, and it separates "works" from "feels live." Let me answer honestly, including where our current code stands and where the genuine tradeoff is.

## First: is the notification API "already done"?

Partially. The **data model** exists (`notifications` collection + outbox worker) and the **pending queue** exists (`GET /kyc/pending`, paginated with `meta.total`). But there is **no live-count endpoint and no real-time push surface yet** — today it's pull-only. So for a live badge, we do need to add something. Not much, but not zero.

## How to get a live "33 in queue" badge — three mechanisms

**The badge is always a COUNT query.** The source of truth is `COUNT(status=PENDING within my scope)` in Mongo. The only question is *how the frontend learns the number changed.* Three ways, cheapest first:

**A. Polling (simplest, works everywhere)**
Frontend calls a cheap `GET /kyc/pending/count` every 15–30s. The badge updates within one interval. For KYC approval this is genuinely enough — nobody is hurt if "33 → 34" shows up 15 seconds late. No persistent connections, no extra infra, and it's correct under *any* deployment (multiple servers, load balancer — doesn't matter). ~90% of the "live" feeling for ~5% of the work.

**B. Server-Sent Events (SSE) — true push, no refresh**
The client opens one long-lived HTTP connection (`GET /kyc/events`, `text/event-stream`). When a KYC is submitted, the service publishes to our in-process **eventbus**; an SSE hub subscribed to that topic pushes a nudge to the connected OMs in scope, and the badge updates **instantly**. SSE is the right fit here because a badge only needs server→client (one-way), it runs over plain HTTP, and it auto-reconnects. This is the "manager already has the dashboard open and the number ticks up by itself" experience.

**C. WebSocket** — bidirectional. Overkill for a badge (you don't need client→server). Save it for genuinely two-way real-time later.

## The "33 in queue AND 33 in DB" sync concern — the robust pattern

Don't push the *computed number*. Push a **nudge** ("something changed"), and let the client **re-fetch the authoritative count**. If you push deltas instead, a single missed event drifts the badge out of sync with the DB forever. "Nudge → re-count" always converges to DB truth — whether you poll or push.

## The honest catch — this is where Redis actually enters

With **one API instance**, SSE + our in-process eventbus works today, no Redis. But the moment you run **multiple API replicas behind a load balancer**: the OM's SSE connection lives on server A, while the KYC submission might hit server B — and B's in-process eventbus can't reach A's connection. *That's* the real trigger for Redis (or NATS) pub/sub: a shared bus to fan events across instances. So:

- **Polling** → correct under any topology, single or multi-replica, no Redis. Ever.
- **SSE, single instance** → works now, no Redis.
- **SSE, multi-instance** → needs Redis/NATS pub/sub as the cross-node fan-out.

## My recommendation

Start with **B-without-the-infra-tax**: add `GET /kyc/pending/count` now (a cheap indexed count), and have the dashboard **poll it every ~20s**. Live-enough, zero new dependencies, survives going multi-replica untouched. Then, *if and when* "instant" becomes a real product ask, layer SSE on top driven by the eventbus — and only reach for Redis pub/sub at the point you're actually running more than one API instance.

Concretely I'd add: a `pending_count` endpoint (reuses the existing scope filter from `listPendingKYC`), and optionally a generalized `GET /notifications/unread-count` if you want the same badge pattern for other roles (payout alerts, safety blocks). Both are small and I can verify them against the smoke suite.

**Which way do you want to go** — (1) count endpoint + polling now (my rec), or (2) go straight to SSE real-time push? If you're planning to run multiple API replicas soon, tell me, because that decides whether SSE needs Redis from day one.

The key fact is that HTTP is request→response — the server **cannot** reach into an already-rendered dashboard on its own. So there are only two ways the number can change on a screen that's just sitting there open:

1. **The dashboard keeps asking** → **polling.** It quietly calls `GET /kyc/pending/count` every ~20s in the background and repaints the badge. To the manager it looks live (33 → 34 appears on its own). No refresh, no persistent connection, works under any deployment.

This is "truly live," and needs the eventbus (and Redis/NATS only once you run multiple API servers).

There's no third option — a plain loaded page can't update itself unless it either re-asks (poll) or holds a channel (push). Everything else is a variation of those two.

**For a KYC approval badge, polling is the right call** — an update landing 15 seconds later hurts nobody, it needs just one small count endpoint, and it survives you scaling to multiple servers with zero changes. Reserve SSE for when "instant, to-the-second" becomes an actual product requirement.

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-07-06 08:30:40Z)**_

Honest answer: **Kafka doesn't actually solve this problem** — and for the badge specifically, it's the wrong layer. Let me explain why, because it's a common and reasonable instinct.

## The thing Kafka can't do

**Kafka cannot talk to a browser.** A dashboard in a browser cannot subscribe to a Kafka topic. So even with Kafka in the stack, the manager's open dashboard *still* only updates via **polling or SSE/WebSocket** — the last mile from your API to the browser is unchanged. Kafka would sit entirely server-side. So for "make the 33 tick up on screen," Kafka adds a broker cluster and changes nothing about the actual mechanism you need.

## What Kafka would actually be competing to do

Kafka is only in the conversation for the **server-side, cross-instance fan-out** — the part where "a KYC was submitted on API server B" needs to reach "the SSE connection held open on API server A." For *that* role, you're choosing between:

| | Weight | Best at |
|---|---|---|
| **Redis pub/sub** | light | fire-and-forget nudges ("something changed, re-count") — ephemeral, lowest latency |
| **NATS** | light | same, slightly richer; JetStream adds durability if needed |
| **Kafka** | heavy | **durable, replayable, ordered** event streams that many independent services consume and must never lose |

For "nudge the dashboards," Redis/NATS win — Kafka's durability and partitioning are dead weight for an ephemeral badge signal.

## Where Kafka *is* genuinely the right answer (and it's already planned)

Kafka earns its keep as the **durable event backbone between microservices** — and our architecture is already built for it. The blueprint names Kafka/NATS as the event bus (§15), and our in-process `eventbus` is explicitly the stand-in that gets swapped for it when this splits into services. That's the real Kafka use case here: **pour recorded, invoice issued, gate blocked, settlement executed** flowing between services as a durable, replayable log that provenance/analytics/multiple consumers all read — audit-grade, never lost, replayable for recovery. That's Kafka's sweet spot. A KYC badge counter is not.

## So, the recommendation

- **For the live badge:** polling a `GET /kyc/pending/count` — still the right call. Kafka wouldn't even remove the browser-side piece.
- **Kafka enters** when you (a) split the monolith into microservices and (b) need durable, replayable, multi-consumer business events — not before. Adding a Kafka cluster to a single-instance modular monolith is a large ops burden (brokers, KRaft, partitions, consumer groups) for zero current benefit; the in-process eventbus already does that job today.
- **If you go real-time SSE across multiple API replicas** before you're on microservices, reach for **Redis pub/sub** (lightest) for the fan-out, not Kafka.

Bottom line: Kafka is a great tool that's genuinely in this system's future — as the inter-service event spine, not as the way to light up a dashboard number. For the badge, polling now; Kafka when microservices + durable events, which is a P2/P3 milestone, not today.

## Now the real question: monolith or microservices?

**My straight recommendation: stay on the modular monolith. Do not switch to microservices now.** And I say that specifically *because* you want best latency + scalability — here's the honest engineering reality:

**Microservices make latency worse, not better.** A monolith calls a module in-process (nanoseconds). Split into services, that same call becomes a network hop + serialization + retry/timeout handling (milliseconds, and new failure modes). So for *latency*, a well-built monolith wins. Microservices trade latency away in exchange for independent scaling and deployment — that's the deal, and it's only worth it when you actually need that.

**Scalability doesn't require microservices.** Our backend is already **stateless** — auth is JWT, no server-side session, all state in Mongo. That means you scale it the easy way: run N copies behind a load balancer and add more when traffic grows. 1cr+ users is handled by *replicas of the monolith + scaling MongoDB*, not by splitting the code. You already have the two things that matter for per-request speed: an index on every hot path, and in-process caches for the org tree and feature flags.

**The best-latency, best-scale setup for this app, today:**
- Run the monolith as **multiple stateless replicas** (Kubernetes deployment + autoscaling) behind a load balancer.
- **MongoDB replica set** for HA now → **shard** when write volume demands it (shard pours by `dcs_id`+date — the natural key).
- A **CDN / gateway cache** in front of the read-heavy public endpoints (the QR scan) — that's your consumer-facing spike absorber.
- The one global serialization point at true national scale is the provenance ledger's sequence — already documented; partition it (per-entity chains) if/when you get there.

That gives you in-process speed *and* horizontal scale without the distributed-systems tax (sagas, eventual consistency, service mesh, distributed tracing, painful local dev).

**Here's the key thing — you already bought the microservices option without paying for it.** We deliberately built a *modular monolith*: 10 modules with hard boundaries, zero cross-module imports, all cross-module talk through the eventbus. Each module maps 1:1 to a future service. So when you *do* have a real reason to split, the extraction is mechanical: lift a module into its own service, swap its in-process eventbus calls for Kafka/NATS topics, done. You keep optionality without the ops cost today.

**When to actually split** (the real triggers — none of which are "for speed"):
- A specific module's load diverges hard from the rest and needs to scale independently — for us the likely first candidate is the **public QR scan/trace** (read-heavy, consumer-facing, spiky) or **pour ingest** (write-spiky at shift times). Extract *that one* when metrics prove it.
- Multiple teams stepping on each other in one codebase (organizational, not technical).
- Fault isolation / different resource profiles (e.g. OCR needing GPUs).

Until one of those is *measured*, splitting is premature — it adds latency and operational burden for benefits you're not yet using.

**Bottom line:** for best time-to-market, lowest latency, and real scalability, the answer is **modular monolith + horizontal replicas + scaled MongoDB now**, and **extract services one at a time only when a specific bottleneck demands it** — which our architecture is already shaped to let you do cleanly. Kafka and the first service extraction are the same milestone (P2/P3), not today's move.

Want me to write this scaling/deployment path into `TECHNICAL_NOTES.md` as an explicit "how to scale this" section — replicas, Mongo sharding, the CDN-for-QR note, and the service-extraction order — so it's on record for when you hit that point?

You invited me to intervene, so I will — and here's the key correction before I build: **for "only 1 completes when two act at once," Redis and Kafka are the wrong tools, and using them here would be *less* correct than the fix I'm about to make.** Let me build the right thing and explain.

The reason: your duplicacy case is two people approving **the same single record**. MongoDB gives you an atomic guard for exactly that — put the state check *inside* the update (`update where _id=X AND status=PENDING`). Only one write matches; the second matches zero rows and gets a 409. That's **stronger** than a Redis lock, because the guard lives on the source of truth itself — a Redis lock can drift from the DB (process dies holding the lock → either deadlock or a TTL expiry that lets a duplicate through). Redis locks are the right tool when you're protecting something that *isn't* one DB row (a cron job across the fleet, a multi-resource action). Kafka is an event stream, not a lock — it can't prevent concurrent writes at all.

So: **duplicacy → Mongo atomic guarded updates** (building now), and **live stream → SSE** (right tool, server→client, no new dependency), with a clean seam so it becomes Redis-pub/sub-backed *only when you go multi-replica*. Let me read the current code and build it:

// rejectKYCRecord flips a PENDING record to REJECTED with the reviewer stamp
// and reason. Same concurrency semantics as approveKYCRecord.
func (r *repository) rejectKYCRecord(ctx context.Context, id, reviewedBy primitive.ObjectID, reviewerRole, reason string, now time.Time) (*domain.KYCRecord, error) {
	filter := bson.D{
		{Key: "_id", Value: id},
		{Key: "status", Value: domain.KYCStatusPending},
	}
	update := bson.D{{Key: "$set", Value: bson.D{
		{Key: "status", Value: domain.KYCStatusRejected},
		{Key: "rejection_reason", Value: reason},
		{Key: "reviewed_by", Value: reviewedBy},
		{Key: "reviewed_by_role", Value: reviewerRole},
		{Key: "reviewed_at", Value: now},
		{Key: "updated_at", Value: now},
	}}}
	opts := options.FindOneAndUpdate().SetReturnDocument(options.After)
	var rec domain.KYCRecord
	err := r.kycRecords.FindOneAndUpdate(ctx, filter, update, opts).Decode(&rec)
	if errors.Is(err, mongo.ErrNoDocuments) {
		return nil, httpx.NotFound("pending kyc record")
	}
	if err != nil {
		return nil, httpx.Internal(fmt.Errorf("reject kyc record: %w", err))
	}
	return &rec, nil
}

1	// Package eventbus is the in-process pub/sub seam between modules
2	// (e.g. settlement executed → notifications module queues the SMS).
3	// It deliberately mirrors a message-broker API: when the platform splits
4	// into microservices, this interface is re-implemented over Kafka/NATS
5	// (blueprint §15) without touching module code.
6	package eventbus
7	
8	import (
9		"context"
10		"log/slog"
11		"sync"
12		"time"
13	)
14	
15	// Topics published across module seams.
16	const (
17		TopicPourRecorded       = "pour.recorded"
18		TopicInvoiceIssued      = "invoice.issued"
19		TopicGateBlocked        = "qc.gate_blocked"
20		TopicSettlementExecuted = "settlement.executed"
21		TopicPayoutCredited     = "payout.credited"
22		TopicMVUDispatched      = "mvu.dispatched"
23	)
24	
25	// Handler consumes a published event. Payload types are documented per topic
26	// by the publishing module.
27	type Handler func(ctx context.Context, topic string, payload any)
28	
29	// Bus is a minimal async pub/sub.
30	type Bus struct {
31		log *slog.Logger
32	
33		mu   sync.RWMutex
34		subs map[string][]Handler
35	}
36	
37	// New builds an empty bus.
38	func New(log *slog.Logger) *Bus {
39		return &Bus{log: log, subs: make(map[string][]Handler)}
40	}
41	
42	// Subscribe registers a handler for a topic. Call during module wiring only
43	// (not concurrently with Publish traffic).
44	func (b *Bus) Subscribe(topic string, h Handler) {
45		b.mu.Lock()
46		defer b.mu.Unlock()
47		b.subs[topic] = append(b.subs[topic], h)
48	}
49	
50	// Publish dispatches asynchronously: each handler runs on its own goroutine
51	// with a bounded context and panic isolation, so a slow or broken subscriber
52	// can never stall the request path.
53	func (b *Bus) Publish(topic string, payload any) {
54		b.mu.RLock()
55		handlers := b.subs[topic]
56		b.mu.RUnlock()
57	
58		for _, h := range handlers {
59			h := h
60			go func() {
61				ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15*time.Second)
62				defer cancel()
63				defer func() {
64					if rec := recover(); rec != nil {
65						b.log.Error("eventbus handler panic",
66							slog.String("topic", topic), slog.Any("panic", rec))
67					}
68				}()
69				h(ctx, topic, payload)
70			}()
71		}
72	}
73

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-07-06 08:58:37Z)**_

<tool-use data-tool-type="write" data-tool-name="Write"><details>
<summary>Tool use: **Write**</summary>

```go
// Package sse implements a Server-Sent Events hub for pushing live updates to
// dashboards that are already open — e.g. an Organising Manager's "pending KYC:
// 33" badge ticking up without a refresh.
//
// Why SSE, not WebSocket: a dashboard badge is a one-way, server→client signal.
// SSE runs over plain HTTP (no new dependency), auto-reconnects in the browser,
// and is far simpler than a WebSocket. It cannot talk to a browser any more
// directly than that — the whole point is the server pushing down an open HTTP
// connection.
//
// Delivery model — "nudge, then re-count": the hub pushes a lightweight event
// (e.g. "kyc.pending.changed"), and the client re-fetches the authoritative,
// org-scoped count from its normal REST endpoint. The nudge is never trusted as
// the number itself, so a slightly-broad nudge is harmless — the scoped count
// query is the source of truth and can never drift.
//
// Single-instance scope: this hub fans out within ONE process. When the API
// runs as multiple replicas, an event raised on replica B must reach a client
// connected to replica A — at that point WireToBus is re-pointed at a shared
// pub/sub (Redis pub/sub or NATS), and nothing else changes. That is the ONLY
// place multi-node real-time needs external infrastructure; the atomic
// duplicate-prevention guarantees live entirely in MongoDB and are unaffected.
package sse

import (
	"log/slog"
	"sync"

	"github.com/google/uuid"
)

// Event is one message pushed to matching clients.
type Event struct {
	Type string `json:"type"` // e.g. "kyc.pending.changed"
	Data any    `json:"data,omitempty"`
	// Roles restricts delivery to clients holding one of these role codes.
	// Empty means "every connected client". Because clients re-fetch a scoped
	// count on receipt, role-level targeting is sufficient — over-delivery only
	// costs a harmless re-count, never a wrong number.
	Roles []string `json:"-"`
}

// Client is one connected dashboard. send is buffered and lossy by design:
// if a slow client's buffer is full we drop the nudge rather than block the
// hub — the next nudge (or the client's periodic poll) re-syncs it.
type Client struct {
	ID        string
	PartyID   string
	RoleCode  string
	OrgUnitID string
	send      chan Event
}

// Events is the channel the HTTP handler ranges over to write the stream.
func (c *Client) Events() <-chan Event { return c.send }

const clientBuffer = 16

// Hub tracks connected clients and fans events out to them.
type Hub struct {
	log *slog.Logger

	mu      sync.RWMutex
	clients map[string]*Client
}

// NewHub builds an empty hub.
func NewHub(log *slog.Logger) *Hub {
	return &Hub{log: log, clients: make(map[string]*Client)}
}

// Register adds a client and returns it. The caller (HTTP handler) must call
// Unregister when the connection closes.
func (h *Hub) Register(partyID, roleCode, orgUnitID string) *Client {
	c := &Client{
		ID:        uuid.NewString(),
		PartyID:   partyID,
		RoleCode:  roleCode,
		OrgUnitID: orgUnitID,
		send:      make(chan Event, clientBuffer),
	}
	h.mu.Lock()
	h.clients[c.ID] = c
	n := len(h.clients)
	h.mu.Unlock()
	h.log.Debug("sse client connected",
		slog.String("client_id", c.ID), slog.String("role", roleCode), slog.Int("connections", n))
	return c
}

// Unregister removes a client and closes its channel. Safe to call once.
func (h *Hub) Unregister(id string) {
	h.mu.Lock()
	c, ok := h.clients[id]
	if ok {
		delete(h.clients, id)
	}
	n := len(h.clients)
	h.mu.Unlock()
	if ok {
		close(c.send)
		h.log.Debug("sse client disconnected",
			slog.String("client_id", id), slog.Int("connections", n))
	}
}

// Broadcast delivers ev to every matching client with a non-blocking send.
func (h *Hub) Broadcast(ev Event) {
	h.mu.RLock()
	defer h.mu.RUnlock()
	delivered, dropped := 0, 0
	for _, c := range h.clients {
		if !roleMatches(ev.Roles, c.RoleCode) {
			continue
		}
		select {
		case c.send <- ev:
			delivered++
		default:
			dropped++ // buffer full — client is slow; the next nudge re-syncs it
		}
	}
	if delivered > 0 || dropped > 0 {
		h.log.Debug("sse broadcast",
			slog.String("type", ev.Type), slog.Int("delivered", delivered), slog.Int("dropped", dropped))
	}
}

// ConnectionCount reports currently-connected clients (metrics/debugging).
func (h *Hub) ConnectionCount() int {
	h.mu.RLock()
	defer h.mu.RUnlock()
	return len(h.clients)
}

func roleMatches(roles []string, role string) bool {
	if len(roles) == 0 {
		return true
	}
	for _, r := range roles {
		if r == role {
			return true
		}
	}
	return false
}

package sse

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"time"

	"github.com/pyaas/saathi-backend/internal/platform/auth"
	"github.com/pyaas/saathi-backend/internal/platform/httpx"
)

// heartbeatInterval keeps the connection alive through proxies/load balancers
// that would otherwise reap an idle stream.
const heartbeatInterval = 25 * time.Second

// StreamHandler returns the HTTP handler for GET /events/stream. It must be
// mounted behind Authenticate (it reads the actor from the request context).
// The connection stays open until the client disconnects or the server shuts
// down; on either the client is unregistered, so no goroutine or channel leaks.
func StreamHandler(hub *Hub) http.HandlerFunc {
	return func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		actor, ok := auth.ActorFrom(r.Context())
		if !ok {
			httpx.Error(w, r, httpx.Unauthorized("authentication required"))
			return
		}
		flusher, ok := w.(http.Flusher)
		if !ok {
			httpx.Error(w, r, httpx.Internal(fmt.Errorf("streaming unsupported by this server")))
			return
		}

		w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
		w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-cache")
		w.Header().Set("Connection", "keep-alive")
		w.Header().Set("X-Accel-Buffering", "no") // disable nginx buffering
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)

		client := hub.Register(actor.PartyID, actor.RoleCode, actor.OrgUnitID)
		defer hub.Unregister(client.ID)

		// Opening frame so the client knows the stream is live and can render
		// its first badge value from its normal REST count call.
		writeSSE(w, "ready", map[string]any{"connected": true})
		flusher.Flush()

		heartbeat := time.NewTicker(heartbeatInterval)
		defer heartbeat.Stop()

		for {
			select {
			case <-r.Context().Done():
				return // client disconnected — defer Unregister cleans up
			case ev, open := <-client.Events():
				if !open {
					return // hub closed this client (server shutdown)
				}
				writeSSE(w, ev.Type, ev.Data)
				flusher.Flush()
			case <-heartbeat.C:
				// SSE comment line — ignored by clients, keeps the socket warm.
				fmt.Fprint(w, ": ping\n\n")
				flusher.Flush()
			}
		}
	}
}

// writeSSE encodes one SSE frame: an event name + a JSON data line.
func writeSSE(w http.ResponseWriter, event string, data any) {
	payload, err := json.Marshal(data)
	if err != nil {
		payload = []byte("{}")
	}
	fmt.Fprintf(w, "event: %s\ndata: %s\n\n", event, payload)
}

func (s *service) kycSubjectInScope(ctx context.Context, actor auth.Actor, subjectPartyID primitive.ObjectID) (bool, error) {
	if actor.RoleCode == domain.RoleSuperAdmin || actor.RoleCode == domain.RoleStateAuditor {
		return true, nil
	}
	assignments, err := s.repo.listActiveAssignments(ctx, subjectPartyID)
	if err != nil {
		return false, err
	}
	for _, ra := range assignments {
		if s.deps.Orgs.RequireInScope(ctx, actor, ra.OrgUnitID) == nil {
			return true, nil
		}
	}
	return false, nil
}

func (h *handler) listPendingKYC(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	actor, ok := actorOr401(w, r)
	if !ok {
		return
	}
	page := httpx.ParsePage(r)
	items, total, err := h.svc.listPendingKYC(r.Context(), actor, page)
	if err != nil {
		httpx.Error(w, r, err)
		return
	}
	httpx.JSONMeta(w, http.StatusOK, items, listMeta{Limit: page.Limit, Offset: page.Offset, Total: total})
}

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-07-06 09:21:33Z)**_

I'll wait for that run to complete. Meanwhile, let me address your Redis question directly with the honest expert answer — because it deserves more than "it costs too much" (cost was never my reason):

## What's *actually* stopping me from adding Redis for the duplicacy problem

**Correctness, not cost.** For "two people act at once, only one completes," a Redis lock is *weaker* than what MongoDB already gives you — and adding it would make the system **less** robust, not more. Here's the real engineering reason a senior would push back:

- **The database is the single source of truth. A Redis lock is a *second* source of truth that can disagree with it.** With the Mongo atomic guard (`update where status=PENDING`), the check and the write are *one indivisible operation* — there is no gap for a second actor to slip through. With a Redis lock, you have two steps: "acquire lock in Redis" then "write to Mongo." Now failure modes appear that didn't exist before: the process dies holding the lock (deadlock, or a TTL expires and lets a duplicate through), Redis and Mongo momentarily disagree, network partition between them. Distributed locks (Redlock) are famously subtle — Martin Kleppmann's well-known critique is exactly about this. You'd be adding a whole failure surface to *weaken* a guarantee you already have for free.
- **The rule of thumb:** if the thing you're protecting is a **single database row**, the database's own atomic conditional update is always the most robust answer. Redis locks are for coordinating things that *aren't* one row — "only one worker in the fleet runs this nightly job," or an action spanning multiple services/resources.

So me *not* reaching for Redis here isn't frugality — it's choosing the more robust primitive. An expert reaches for the lightest tool that gives the strongest guarantee, and here that's the DB.

## Where Redis genuinely *does* make this backend more robust (and I'll add it)

Since you want a production-grade, scalable pipeline and cost is no object, Redis earns a real place — just not as a lock. Two genuine roles, both at **multi-replica scale**:

1. **Distributed rate limiting** — today rate limiting is per-instance in memory. When you run N replicas behind a load balancer, an attacker's requests spread across instances and each only sees a fraction. A shared Redis token-bucket gives *global* abuse protection. This is real robustness.
2. **SSE fan-out across replicas** — the live badge I just built works within one process. Across replicas, a KYC submitted on server B must nudge a dashboard connected to server A. Redis pub/sub (or NATS) is the cross-node bus for that.

The expert way to add these: **behind an interface, with an in-memory default and a Redis backend that activates when `REDIS_URL` is set** — so dev/tests stay Redis-free and green, and production flips it on. That's dependency inversion: the code is Redis-ready without being Redis-coupled.

I'll wait for the smoke run to confirm the live-badge + concurrency proof is green, then implement the Redis-backed distributed rate limiter behind that abstraction and report the full production-hardening picture.

```go
// Package ratelimit provides pluggable request rate limiting behind a single
// interface, so the HTTP middleware stays backend-agnostic.
//
// Two backends ship:
//   - Memory  — a per-key token bucket in process memory. Correct and fastest
//     for a SINGLE instance; each replica limits only the traffic it sees.
//   - Redis   — a shared token bucket in Redis, evaluated atomically by a Lua
//     script. Gives GLOBAL fairness across many API replicas — the reason to
//     reach for Redis in this system (blueprint §6/§17: rate-limiting at the
//     edge). This is a legitimate Redis use; duplicate-prevention is NOT (that
//     lives in MongoDB's atomic conditional updates, which are strictly safer
//     than any external lock).
//
// Selection is by configuration: set REDIS_URL and the server uses Redis,
// otherwise it falls back to Memory. Dev and tests need no Redis.
package ratelimit

import "context"

// Limiter decides whether a request keyed by `key` (typically the client IP)
// may proceed right now. Allow must be safe for concurrent use.
type Limiter interface {
	// Allow reports whether one unit of quota is available for key, consuming
	// it when true. On backend errors implementations fail OPEN (return true)
	// so a rate-limiter outage never takes down the API.
	Allow(ctx context.Context, key string) bool
	// Kind names the backend for logging/metrics ("memory" | "redis").
	Kind() string
}

```

package ratelimit

import (
	"context"
	"sync"
	"time"

	"golang.org/x/time/rate"
)

// Memory is an in-process, per-key token-bucket limiter. Each API instance
// enforces its own limit; at multi-replica scale switch to Redis for global
// fairness. A janitor evicts idle buckets so the map cannot grow unbounded.
type Memory struct {
	rps   float64
	burst int

	mu      sync.Mutex
	buckets map[string]*memBucket
}

type memBucket struct {
	lim  *rate.Limiter
	seen time.Time
}

// NewMemory builds an in-process limiter allowing `rps` requests/second per key
// with a `burst` allowance, and starts the idle-bucket janitor.
func NewMemory(rps float64, burst int) *Memory {
	m := &Memory{rps: rps, burst: burst, buckets: make(map[string]*memBucket)}
	go m.janitor()
	return m
}

// Allow consumes one token for key, refilling per the configured rate.
func (m *Memory) Allow(_ context.Context, key string) bool {
	m.mu.Lock()
	b, ok := m.buckets[key]
	if !ok {
		b = &memBucket{lim: rate.NewLimiter(rate.Limit(m.rps), m.burst)}
		m.buckets[key] = b
	}
	b.seen = time.Now()
	m.mu.Unlock()
	return b.lim.Allow()
}

// Kind identifies the backend.
func (m *Memory) Kind() string { return "memory" }

func (m *Memory) janitor() {
	for range time.Tick(5 * time.Minute) {
		m.mu.Lock()
		for key, b := range m.buckets {
			if time.Since(b.seen) > 10*time.Minute {
				delete(m.buckets, key)
			}
		}
		m.mu.Unlock()
	}
}

```

package ratelimit

import (
	"context"
	"log/slog"
	"time"

	"github.com/redis/go-redis/v9"
)

// tokenBucketLua is an atomic token-bucket evaluated entirely inside Redis, so
// concurrent requests from many API replicas can never over-admit. State per
// key is a hash {tokens, ts}; each call refills by elapsed time, then spends
// one token if available. The key auto-expires once idle long enough to have
// refilled a full burst, so buckets never leak.
//
//	KEYS[1] = bucket key
//	ARGV[1] = rate (tokens/sec)  ARGV[2] = burst
//	ARGV[3] = now (unix seconds, float)  ARGV[4] = requested (1)
//	returns 1 = allowed, 0 = denied
const tokenBucketLua = `
local key   = KEYS[1]
local rate  = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local burst = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now   = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local req   = tonumber(ARGV[4])

local h = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(h[1])
local ts = tonumber(h[2])
if tokens == nil then tokens = burst; ts = now end

local delta = now - ts
if delta < 0 then delta = 0 end
tokens = math.min(burst, tokens + delta * rate)

local allowed = 0
if tokens >= req then tokens = tokens - req; allowed = 1 end

redis.call('HSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
local ttl = math.ceil(burst / rate) + 1
redis.call('EXPIRE', key, ttl)
return allowed
`

// Redis is a shared token-bucket limiter backed by Redis — global fairness
// across every API replica. Fails OPEN on any Redis error so a cache outage
// degrades to "no limiting" rather than an outage of the API itself.
type Redis struct {
	client *redis.Client
	script *redis.Script
	rps    float64
	burst  int
	prefix string
	log    *slog.Logger
}

// NewRedis builds a Redis-backed limiter. The caller owns the *redis.Client
// lifecycle (Ping on boot, Close on shutdown).
func NewRedis(client *redis.Client, rps float64, burst int, log *slog.Logger) *Redis {
	return &Redis{
		client: client,
		script: redis.NewScript(tokenBucketLua),
		rps:    rps,
		burst:  burst,
		prefix: "saathi:rl:",
		log:    log,
	}
}

// Allow consumes one token for key across the shared bucket.
func (r *Redis) Allow(ctx context.Context, key string) bool {
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 100*time.Millisecond)
	defer cancel()

	now := float64(time.Now().UnixNano()) / 1e9
	res, err := r.script.Run(ctx, r.client,
		[]string{r.prefix + key},
		r.rps, r.burst, now, 1,
	).Int()
	if err != nil {
		// Fail open: never let a limiter outage become an API outage.
		r.log.Warn("redis rate limiter error — failing open", slog.String("key", key), slog.Any("err", err))
		return true
	}
	return res == 1
}

// Kind identifies the backend.
func (r *Redis) Kind() string { return "redis" }

```

package middleware

import (
	"net"
	"net/http"

	"github.com/pyaas/saathi-backend/internal/platform/httpx"
	"github.com/pyaas/saathi-backend/internal/platform/ratelimit"
)

// RateLimit throttles requests per client IP using the supplied Limiter. The
// backend (in-process or Redis-shared) is chosen at wiring time in cmd/server,
// so this middleware is backend-agnostic — the same code path defends a single
// instance or a whole replica fleet.
func RateLimit(limiter ratelimit.Limiter) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			ip, _, err := net.SplitHostPort(r.RemoteAddr)
			if err != nil {
				ip = r.RemoteAddr
			}
			if !limiter.Allow(r.Context(), ip) {
				httpx.Error(w, r, httpx.TooManyRequests("too many requests — slow down"))
				return
			}
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
		})
	}
}

```

Done — and I gave you the honest expert answer on Redis, then built the genuinely-robust version of it. Everything verified by my own hands: **build ✅ · vet ✅ · 11 test packages ✅ · gofmt ✅ · full 23-step smoke ✅**.

## What I built (the live stream + the duplicacy guarantee)

**1. Live dashboard badge — SSE, proven working.** New `GET /api/v1/events/stream` (Server-Sent Events) + `GET /kyc/pending/count`. When any KYC is submitted/approved/rejected, the server pushes a `kyc.pending.changed` nudge down every open reviewer dashboard, which re-fetches its scoped count — the badge ticks up **with no refresh**. Smoke step 23 proved it end-to-end: the stream delivered `event: ready` then `event: kyc.pending.changed`, and the badge went **0 → 1** live.

**2. Duplicacy — proven, and done the *correct* way (MongoDB, not Redis).** Smoke step 22 fires two approvals at the same KYC record simultaneously: results came back **`200` and `409`** — exactly one completed. This is the atomic status-guarded update (`update where status=PENDING`), which I verified is already the pattern across KYC, settlement, and the BMC-lot→batch claim.

**3. Redis — added where it genuinely makes this robust.** A **distributed rate limiter** behind a clean interface: in-memory by default (dev/tests stay Redis-free and green), shared Redis token-bucket when `REDIS_URL` is set. I tested the Redis path against your live local Redis: 30 rapid requests → exactly **5×200 + 25×429**, with the bucket key `saathi:rl:::1` created in Redis. It fails *open* on a Redis outage so the limiter can never take down the API. Added to `docker-compose.yml` and `.env.example`.

## The honest Redis position (why it's not for locks)

Not adding Redis for duplicacy was a **correctness** decision, not a cost one. A Redis lock is a *second* source of truth that can drift from the DB (process dies holding the lock → deadlock or a TTL that lets duplicates through). Mongo's single-document atomic update makes the check-and-write one indivisible operation — strictly safer. Redis earns its place for **cross-replica** concerns (rate limiting now; SSE fan-out and shared cache when you scale out), and I built the seams so those flip on with config, no rewrites.

## Files added
- `internal/platform/sse/` — hub + handler (non-blocking, heartbeats, disconnect cleanup)
- `internal/platform/ratelimit/` — `Limiter` interface + `memory` + `redis` (atomic Lua token bucket)
- Docs updated: `strict_brief.md` gained §1.8 (concurrency), §1.9 (real-time/SSE), §1.10 (rate limiting) + the new endpoints.

Here's everything added in this round, grouped by feature — ready to drop into a commit message or changelog:

## Feature: Live dashboard notifications (SSE) + real-time KYC badge

**New real-time streaming (`internal/platform/sse/`)**
- `hub.go` — Server-Sent Events hub: tracks connected dashboards, non-blocking lossy sends (a slow client never blocks the hub), role-targeted broadcast, disconnect cleanup (no goroutine/channel leaks), connection count.
- `handler.go` — the `GET /api/v1/events/stream` handler: SSE headers, 25s heartbeats, per-connection write-deadline cleared (so the stream outlives the server's 60s write timeout), teardown on client disconnect.

**New live badge endpoint (`identity` module)**
- `GET /api/v1/kyc/pending/count` — scoped pending-KYC count for the reviewer's dashboard badge (`{count, capped}`), reusing the exact scope logic of `/kyc/pending` so badge and list always agree.
- On KYC submit/approve/reject, identity now publishes a `kyc.queue_changed` event → the hub nudges every open reviewer dashboard → it re-fetches the scoped count and the badge updates **without a refresh**.
- New eventbus topic `TopicKYCQueueChanged` + `KYCQueueEvent` payload; the KYC→SSE bridge wired in `cmd/server`.

## Feature: Distributed rate limiting (Redis, pluggable)

**New rate-limit abstraction (`internal/platform/ratelimit/`)**
- `limiter.go` — `Limiter` interface (backend-agnostic; fails open).
- `memory.go` — in-process per-IP token bucket (default; single instance) with idle-bucket janitor.
- `redis.go` — shared Redis token bucket via an **atomic Lua script** for global fairness across replicas; auto-expiring keys; fails open on Redis errors so a cache outage can't take down the API.
- Selection by config: `REDIS_URL` set → Redis, else in-process. Middleware (`RateLimit`) now backend-agnostic.
- `cmd/server` connects/pings/closes the Redis client on boot/shutdown; new `REDIS_URL` config; `.env.example` + `docker-compose.yml` gained a `redis:7` service.

## Concurrency / duplicacy guarantee (verified, not added)

- Confirmed the "only one completes" protection is already correct via MongoDB atomic status-guarded updates (KYC approve/reject, settlement execute, BMC-lot→batch claim) — **no Redis lock**, which would be less safe.

## Tests & docs

# Saathi Backend — How It Works (Flow Diagrams)

> **Purpose:** a visual map of how the backend behaves *right now*, so you can review it, spot gaps,
> and decide where to intervene. Every diagram reflects the actual code in `internal/` and `cmd/`.
> Companion docs: [`strict_brief.md`](strict_brief.md) (per-endpoint contract),
> [`WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md`](WORKFLOW_GUIDE.md) (role flows), [`TECHNICAL_NOTES.md`](TECHNICAL_NOTES.md)
> (architecture decisions).
>
> Diagrams are Mermaid — they render in GitHub, GitLab and VS Code.

---

## 1. The whole system at a glance

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph clients["Clients (separate repos)"]
        FE["Farmer / Sacheev / Admin apps\n(role-based dashboards)"]
        PUB["Public QR scan\n(no login)"]
    end

    subgraph api["Saathi API (Go modular monolith — one deployable)"]
        direction TB
        RTR["HTTP Router + global middleware\n(internal/httpapi)"]
        MODS["10 domain modules\n(internal/modules/*)"]
        PLAT["Platform services\n(internal/platform/*)"]
        RTR --> MODS --> PLAT
    end

    subgraph stores["State"]
        MONGO[("MongoDB\n28 collections\n+ provenance ledger")]
        REDIS[("Redis (optional)\nshared rate-limit / future SSE fan-out")]
    end

    FE -->|"REST JSON /api/v1 + JWT"| RTR
    FE -.->|"SSE /events/stream (live badge)"| RTR
    PUB -->|"GET /public/qr/... (no auth)"| RTR
    PLAT --> MONGO
    PLAT --> REDIS

    EXT["Mocked DPI edge:\nAadhaar · Bank · PFMS/DBT ·\nBharat Pashudhan · SMS · Payment Aggregator"]
    PLAT -.->|"single named seams,\nswap mock → real"| EXT
```

**Read this as:** clients hit one Go service over REST (+ an SSE stream for live updates); the service
is internally split into 10 isolated modules over shared platform services; all state lives in MongoDB
(Redis is optional, only for cross-replica concerns); external gov systems sit behind mock seams.

---

## 2. The global request pipeline (every request passes through this)

Order is exactly as wired in `internal/httpapi/router.go`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    IN(["HTTP request"]) --> RID["RequestID\n(correlation id)"]
    RID --> RIP["RealIP"]
    RIP --> MET["Metrics\n(Prometheus)"]
    MET --> LOG["RequestLogger\n(1 structured line/request)"]
    LOG --> RL["RateLimit\n(memory or Redis)"]
    RL --> REC["Recoverer\n(panic → 500)"]
    REC --> TO["Timeout 30s"]
    TO --> BR{"route?"}
    BR -->|"/healthz /readyz\n/metrics /version"| OPS["operational\n(no auth)"]
    BR -->|"/api/v1/public/*"| PUBH["public handlers\n(no auth)"]
    BR -->|"/api/v1/events/stream"| SSEH["Authenticate → SSE stream"]
    BR -->|"/api/v1/* (modules)"| AUD["AuditMutations\n(writes only)"] --> MOD["module route\n(auth + RBAC)"]
    BR -->|"unmatched"| NF["JSON 404 / 405\n(never chi plaintext)"]
```

Key facts to note for analysis:
- **Rate limiting runs before auth** (cheap abuse protection). It's per-IP; `REDIS_URL` makes it shared across replicas.
- **AuditMutations** wraps every state-changing `/api/v1` call — the immutable who-did-what trail.
- **Public routes and the operational endpoints deliberately skip authentication.**
- A single `request_id` threads through the request log and every module log line — that's how you trace one request end-to-end.

---

## 3. Inside a request — the layered flow (handler → service → repo)

Every module follows the same four-file contract. Example: recording a milk pour.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant C as Client
    participant MW as Middleware<br/>(auth + RBAC)
    participant H as handler.go<br/>(HTTP only)
    participant S as service.go<br/>(business logic)
    participant R as repo.go<br/>(Mongo only)
    participant L as Ledger / Bus / Audit
    participant DB as MongoDB

    C->>MW: POST /api/v1/collection/pours + role JWT
    MW->>MW: verify token → Actor on ctx;<br/>RequireRoles(SACHEEV, MILK_TESTER)
    MW->>H: (authorised)
    H->>H: decode JSON, parse ObjectIDs (httpx)
    H->>S: CreatePour(ctx, actor, req)
    S->>S: RequireInScope(dcs) · farmer is member? ·<br/>price via rate chart · plausibility gate
    S->>R: idempotency check (client_event_id)
    R->>DB: findOne / insert
    S->>L: append pour.recorded · publish bus · queue SMS
    L->>DB: provenance event (hash-chained)
    S-->>H: pour struct or *AppError
    H-->>C: JSON envelope {data:...} or {error:...}
```

The rule the whole codebase obeys: **handlers do HTTP, services do logic, repos do Mongo, and modules
never import each other** — cross-module effects go through the event bus.

---

## 4. Identity: login → KYC approval → position → dashboard

This is the onboarding spine (the "which UI does the user get" question).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["POST /auth/otp/request\n+ /auth/otp/verify"] --> B["Party created\ntier MINIMAL · no roles"]
    B --> C{"has a usable role?"}
    C -->|no| D["Frontend shows\n'pending / submit KYC'"]
    D --> E["POST /kyc/aadhaar\n→ KYCRecord PENDING"]
    E --> F["Reviewer: GET /kyc/pending\n(Organising Manager / admin)"]
    F --> G["POST /kyc/{id}/approve\n(atomic: status=PENDING guard)"]
    G --> H["party tier upgraded\n(upward only)"]
    H --> I["Admin: POST /roles/assignments\n= assign the POSITION\n(role_code @ org unit)"]
    I --> C
    C -->|yes| J["GET /auth/roles"]
    J --> K["POST /auth/role/select\n(checks KYC tier ≥ required)"]
    K --> L["ROLE JWT: role_code + org scope"]
    L --> M["Frontend renders THAT dashboard\nfrom role_code"]
```

Analysis hooks:
- A role token is **only** issuable once KYC tier satisfies the role (`403 KYC_TIER_INSUFFICIENT` before approval).
- Position = a `RoleAssignment` row (not a field on the user), so one human can hold several and switch.
- **Open question flagged earlier:** a brand-new party with no assignment is only visible to federation-wide reviewers (Super Admin / PCDF Admin), not a scoped Organising Manager — first-touch KYC routing is a product decision.

---

## 5. The core milk loop (pour → QR → payment) with the safety gate

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["reading\n(anti-tamper)"] --> P["pour\n(idempotent, priced)"]
    P --> INV["same-day invoice"]
    P --> CON["consignment\n(pooling boundary §7.4)"]
    CON --> TRIP["route trip\n+ cold chain"]
    TRIP --> LOT["BMC lot"]
    LOT --> G1{"QC gate\nBMC_RAPID"}
    G1 -->|pass| BAT["processing batch"]
    G1 -->|fail| BLK["BLOCKED\nquarantine + supervisor alert"]
    BAT --> G2{"QC gate\nPLANT_LAB"}
    G2 -->|pass| PL["product lot"]
    G2 -->|fail| BLK
    PL --> QR["signed QR"]
    QR --> SCAN["public scan\nsamiti-set provenance +\nintact hash chain"]
    INV --> SET["settlement\ninitiate → approve → execute\n(dual control)"]
    SET --> PAY["farmer paid + SMS"]

    classDef gate fill:#fde,stroke:#c39;
    class G1,G2 gate;
```

Every box appends a provenance event; a `BLOCKED` subject can never advance (dispatch/batch/product/QR all re-check). FSSAI limits (AFM1 ≤ 0.5 µg/kg, coliform ≤ 10 CFU/ml, phosphatase negative) are enforced in `domain/quality.go`.

---

## 6. Module map + how modules talk (event bus, never direct)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph modules["internal/modules/*  (future microservice seams)"]
        ID["identity\nauth · KYC · roles"]
        OR["orgs"]
        CA["cattle"]
        CO["collection\n(core loop)"]
        LO["logistics"]
        PL["plant"]
        QU["quality\n(gate verdict)"]
        SE["settlement"]
        PT["publictrace"]
        PO["platformops\nadmin · audit · notifications"]
    end

    BUS(["eventbus (in-process pub/sub)\n→ swaps to Kafka/NATS at scale"])

    CO -->|pour.recorded / invoice.issued| BUS
    QU -->|qc.gate_blocked| BUS
    SE -->|payout.credited| BUS
    CA -->|mvu.dispatched| BUS
    ID -->|kyc.queue_changed| BUS

    BUS --> PO
    BUS --> SSE(["SSE hub → live dashboards"])

    PO -.->|queues SMS / notifications| OUTBOX[("notifications\noutbox")]
```

Modules read shared services from one `deps.Deps` container: `JWT, Ledger, Audit, Flags, Orgs, Bus, SSE, RateLimiter, DB, Cfg, Log`.

---

## 7. Real-time: the live "pending KYC" badge (SSE)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant OM as Reviewer dashboard
    participant API as API
    participant BUS as eventbus
    participant HUB as SSE hub
    participant NEW as New user

    OM->>API: GET /events/stream (SSE, held open)
    API->>HUB: register connection (role = reviewer)
    API-->>OM: event: ready
    OM->>API: GET /kyc/pending/count → badge shows N
    NEW->>API: POST /kyc/aadhaar (submits KYC)
    API->>BUS: publish kyc.queue_changed
    BUS->>HUB: broadcast to reviewer roles
    HUB-->>OM: event: kyc.pending.changed  (nudge)
    OM->>API: GET /kyc/pending/count → badge shows N+1
    Note over OM,API: "nudge, then re-count" — the scoped count<br/>query is the source of truth, so the badge<br/>can never drift. No refresh needed.
```

Today the hub fans out within one process. At multi-replica scale the broadcast swaps to Redis pub/sub — no route changes.

---

## 8. Concurrency: "two at once → only one wins" (no Redis lock)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Reviewer A: approve KYC X"] --> DB{{"MongoDB atomic update\nupdate WHERE _id=X AND status=PENDING"}}
    B["Reviewer B: approve KYC X\n(same instant)"] --> DB
    DB -->|matched 1 doc| WIN["one wins → 200\nstatus=VERIFIED"]
    DB -->|matched 0 docs| LOSE["other → 409 KYC_NOT_PENDING"]
```

The state check lives **inside** the update filter, so the check-and-write is one indivisible operation.
Same pattern guards settlement `execute` (with a resume lease) and the BMC-lot→batch claim
(`DISPATCHED → POOLED`, so one lot can't feed two batches). This is safer than a Redis lock — one
source of truth, no lock-vs-DB drift. Proven by smoke step 22 (`200` + `409`).

---

## 9. Data stores (what lives where)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph mongo["MongoDB (single source of truth)"]
        direction TB
        IDENT["parties · role_assignments ·\nkyc_records · consents ·\notp_challenges · refresh_tokens"]
        ORG["org_units (denormalised path[])"]
        LOOP["milk_pours · invoices · rate_charts ·\nanalyzer_readings · dcs_consignments ·\nroute_trips · bmc_lots · processing_batches ·\nproduct_lots · batch_qrs · qc_results"]
        MONEY["settlement_batches · payout_instructions ·\ndbt_requests"]
        HERD["animals · health_events · mvu_cases · education"]
        SYS["provenance_events (hash chain) ·\naudit_logs · notifications · feature_flags · counters"]
    end
    REDIS[("Redis (optional)\nrate-limit buckets")]
    OBJ["Object store (planned)\nanalyzer photos · PoD"]
```

Every `_id` is an ObjectID; every cross-collection reference is an ObjectID (native `$lookup`/populate).
Human-readable keys (`phone`, `code`, `qr_code`, `invoice_number`, `pashu_aadhaar`) are separate unique
indexes. The `provenance_events` collection is append-only and hash-chained.

---

## 10. Where to intervene — analysis checklist

Points a human reviewer should weigh (honest current state):

| Area | Current state | Decision / next step |
|---|---|---|
| **Deployment** | single modular monolith, stateless | scale = N replicas + Mongo replica-set/shard; split a module out only when a bottleneck is measured |
| **Real-time** | SSE within one process | add Redis pub/sub for cross-replica fan-out when >1 replica |
| **Rate limiting** | in-process default; Redis when `REDIS_URL` set | turn on Redis in prod (compose already wired) |
| **First-touch KYC routing** | scoped reviewers can't see assignment-less new parties | product decision: auto-route new KYC to a district queue? |
| **External DPI** | all mocked behind named seams | wire real Aadhaar / bank / PFMS / Bharat Pashudhan / SMS / PA one seam at a time |
| **Notifications** | outbox + manual worker endpoint | move worker to cron/queue; add real SMS provider |
| **Object store** | `photo_object_key` fields exist, no upload endpoint | add S3-compatible presigned upload |
| **Multi-doc invariants** | safe via atomic guards + unique indexes | optional Mongo transactions (needs replica set) to tighten crash windows |
| **Observability** | structured logs + Prometheus metrics + health/ready | add OpenTelemetry tracing when microservices land |
| **CI/CD, IaC, K8s** | Dockerfile + compose only | add pipeline + manifests before go-live |

```toml
# Air — live-reload daemon for the Saathi API (the Go equivalent of nodemon).
# On every save under cmd/ or internal/, Air rebuilds ./cmd/server and restarts
# it, so local changes reflect immediately. Run with `make dev`.
#
# The server does a graceful shutdown on SIGINT, so `send_interrupt = true`
# lets Air close MongoDB/Redis cleanly between reloads instead of hard-killing.
root = "."
tmp_dir = "tmp"

[build]
  # Build only the server (not the seed binary) into the temp dir.
  cmd = "go build -o ./tmp/saathi-server ./cmd/server"
  bin = "./tmp/saathi-server"
  # The binary runs from the repo root, so it picks up .env automatically.
  full_bin = ""
  include_ext = ["go", "toml", "env"]
  include_dir = ["cmd", "internal"]
  exclude_dir = ["bin", "tmp", "vendor", "docs", "scripts", ".git"]
  # Tests don't affect the running server — don't restart on them.
  exclude_regex = ["_test\\.go"]
  # Debounce rapid saves; wait for the build before restarting.
  delay = 800
  stop_on_error = true
  # Graceful restart: SIGINT → our server's shutdown path → then kill if it lingers.
  send_interrupt = true
  kill_delay = "3s"

[log]
  time = true

[misc]
  # Remove ./tmp on exit so the workspace stays clean.
  clean_on_exit = true

```

Done — added the hot-reload daemon and **verified it works end-to-end**.

## What I added

**Air** — the Go equivalent of nodemon/JavaScript daemons. On every file save under `cmd/` or `internal/`, it rebuilds and restarts the server automatically, so your changes reflect immediately.

**Files:**
- **`.air.toml`** — daemon config tuned for this repo: watches `cmd/` + `internal/`, ignores tests/docs/scripts, 800ms debounce, and (nicely) uses `send_interrupt` so it triggers our server's **graceful shutdown** (closes MongoDB/Redis cleanly) between reloads instead of hard-killing.
- **`make dev`** — the one command to use. Auto-installs Air if it's missing, then starts watching.
- **`.gitignore`** — Air's `tmp/` and `build-errors.log` excluded.
- **README** — `make dev` documented in the getting-started block.

## Proof it works

I ran a live test: started `make dev`, then edited the version string in `router.go` while the server was running. Without me touching anything, the running server auto-updated:

```
BEFORE save: "version":"0.1.0-dev"
→ edited router.go
AFTER save:  "version":"0.1.0-HOTRELOAD-OK"     ← reflected automatically
```

Air's log showed `building... running...` on the save. I reverted the test edit, so `router.go` is back to `0.1.0-dev`.

## How you'll use it

```bash
make dev        # start the daemon — leave it running in a terminal
# ... edit any .go file and save ...
# → Air rebuilds + restarts automatically; hit localhost:8080 to see the change
```

Note it reloads the **backend server** (this is a backend repo — no emulator here; the frontend/app lives in its separate repo and would have its own hot-reload). If you later want the daemon to also re-run `make seed` or ping the frontend on reload, I can extend the `.air.toml` post-build hook.

Build is green, no stray processes, still uncommitted.

# Saathi (parag-saathi-fe) — context for every session

Android-first, offline-first mobile app for the Nand Baba Dugdh Mission (PCDF / Parag)
dairy traceability platform. Expo SDK 57 · React Native 0.86 · TypeScript (strict) ·
expo-router · TanStack Query · zustand · i18next (en + हिं). One phone = one identity =
many org-scoped, time-bounded roles.

## Run the app locally (hard-won — follow exactly)

This machine had no PATH wiring; these are required. Run the app as a **dev build** on
the `parag_pixel` emulator (NOT Expo Go — Expo Go SDK 57 segfaults in `libworklets.so`).

```bash
cd ~/parag-saathi-fe
export ANDROID_HOME="$HOME/Library/Android/sdk"
export JAVA_HOME="/Applications/Android Studio.app/Contents/jbr/Contents/Home"
export PATH="/opt/homebrew/bin:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools:$ANDROID_HOME/emulator:$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
emulator -avd parag_pixel &                 # if not already running
npx expo start --dev-client --clear --android
```

- **Watchman is required** (`brew install watchman`) or Metro won't detect saves
  (Node 26 / macOS 26 breaks Metro's fallback watcher). Start Metro with `--clear` so it
  re-arms the Watchman subscription.
- **Hot reload:** edit any `.ts/.tsx` → shows on the emulator in ~1s. Adding a **native**
  dep needs a rebuild (`npx expo run:android`, ~10 min); `.env` / config changes need a
  Metro restart; pulling teammates' new commits may need a **full reload** (emulator
  Cmd+M → Reload).
- **Emulator hardware keyboard** is enabled (`hw.keyboard = yes` in the AVD) so the Mac
  keyboard types into fields.

## Data mode (mock vs http)

`src/core/api/client.ts` defaults `MODE` to **http** (real Go backend). For local dev with
no server, `.env` sets `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_MODE=mock` → runs against the seeded in-app DB
(`src/core/mocks/db.ts`). Mock + http return identical types. **If you see "Something went
wrong" on every action, it's http mode with no backend — set mock in `.env` + restart Metro.**

# Saathi API contract (frontend ↔ backend)

The mobile app ships with an in-app mock backend; flipping
`EXPO_PUBLIC_API_MODE=http` + `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` points the same typed
calls at the real API. **This file is the request-for-implementation for the
backend team.** The authoritative, always-current definitions (exact TS
request/response types + reference semantics in the `mock` bodies) live in
[`src/core/api/endpoints/`](../src/core/api/endpoints/) with the shared domain
model in [`src/core/types/domain.ts`](../src/core/types/domain.ts).

Conventions (matching the implemented backend): success envelope
`{"data": ..., "meta"?}`; error envelope `{"error": {"code", "message", "details"?}}`;
snake_case wire fields (the app maps them to its camelCase domain in
`mapRequest`/`mapResponse` per endpoint); `Authorization: Bearer <access token>`;
rotating refresh tokens via `POST /auth/refresh` (the client auto-refreshes
once on 401 and retries); IDs opaque strings; timestamps ISO-8601.

## Auth / identity (`auth.ts`) - ✅ aligned with `parag-saathi-be` `internal/modules/identity`
| Method & path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `POST /auth/otp/request` | `{phone}` → `{phone, expires_at, dev_otp?}` (dev_otp only in dev mode) |
| `POST /auth/otp/verify` | `{phone, otp}` → `{access_token (SESSION), refresh_token, party}`; find-or-creates the Party on first login (§4.1) |
| `GET /parties/me` | → `{party, assignments (+org_name/org_type/org_code), kyc?}` - feeds the role switcher |
| `POST /auth/role/select` | `{role_assignment_id}` → `{access_token (ROLE-scoped), role_code, org_unit_id}` |
| `POST /auth/refresh` | `{refresh_token}` → rotated token pair (single-flight in the client) |
| `POST /auth/logout` | `{refresh_token}` - revoke (called fire-and-forget on sign-out) |
| `PATCH /parties/me` | `{full_name?, preferred_language?}` |
| `POST /kyc/aadhaar` | `{aadhaar_number, consent, requested_tier}` - number transient, never stored (§18-A) |
| `POST /kyc/bank` | `{account_number, ifsc}` - penny-drop; only masked tail persisted |

## Real-time & live badges (`events.ts` + `sse.ts`) - ✅ PR #2
| Method & path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /events/stream` | Server-Sent Events (bearer-auth). The app streams it via XHR (`core/api/sse.ts`); `useLiveSync` invalidates query caches on `kyc.queue_changed`, `settlement.changed`, `quality.changed`, `pour.recorded`. Heartbeats every ~25s |
| `GET /kyc/pending/count` | `{count, capped}` - scoped pending-KYC badge for reviewer dashboards |

## Org (`org.ts`)
| `GET /org-units?type=` | List org units (FEDERATION/UNION/DCS/BMC/PLANT) |
| `GET /org-units/:id` | One org unit |

## Collections - DCS console (`collections.ts`)
| `GET /dcs/:dcsId/members` | Farmer roster + pouredToday |
| `GET /pours?dcsId&farmerPartyId&date&shift` | Pour list |
| `POST /pours` | Record a pour; server computes rate from the two-axis chart, enforces §8.2 plausibility bounds (`422 IMPLAUSIBLE_READING`), and upserts the same-day DRAFT invoice (§8.1) |
| `POST /pours/ocr-extract` | Photo-OCR bridge: analyzer-screen photo → `{fatPct, snfPct, confidence}` (§8.2) |
| `GET /lots?dcsId&date&status` · `GET /lots/:id` | Consignment lots |
| `POST /lots` | Pool the shift's RECORDED pours into an OPEN lot |
| `POST /lots/:id/dispatch` | OPEN → DISPATCHED; attaches to today's route stop |

## Payments (`payments.ts`) - §8.1 / §18-B
| `GET /invoices?farmerPartyId&dcsId&status&date` | Invoices |
| `POST /dcs/:dcsId/invoices/approve` | Day's DRAFT → APPROVED |
| `POST /invoices/settle` | APPROVED → SETTLED (+UTR); **must remain an authorised human action** |
| `GET /rate-config` · `PUT /rate-config` | Two-axis fat/SNF rate chart |

## Logistics (`logistics.ts`)
| `GET /trips/mine?riderPartyId&date` · `GET /trips?date` | Route manifest |
| `POST /trips/:id/start` | ASSIGNED → IN_PROGRESS |
| `POST /trips/:id/pickup` | Stop pickup + cold-chain temp (`409 LOT_NOT_DISPATCHED` if samiti hasn't dispatched) |
| `POST /trips/:id/deliver` | Pool collected lots into a BMC intake (silo lot) |

## Plant (`plant.ts`) - §8.3 stages
| `GET /intakes?status` | Silo intakes |
| `GET /batches?plantId&stage&qcStatus` · `GET /batches/:id` | Processing batches |
| `POST /batches` | Create batch from intakes (carries contributing DCS set, §7.4) |
| `POST /batches/:id/stage` | Stage transition; **server enforces the QC gate** (`409 QC_GATE_BLOCKED`) |
| `POST /batches/:id/outputs` | Assign product outputs → batch-level QR codes (§8.4) |

## Quality / lab (`quality.ts`) - the safety gate (§8.3)
| `GET /qc/queue` | Batches pending QC + pending parameters |
| `GET /qc/tests?subjectId` | Test results |
| `POST /qc/tests` | Record reading; verdict vs FSSAI limits (AFM1 ≤0.5 µg/kg, coliform ≤10 CFU/ml, TPC, tetracycline MRL, phosphatase-negative). FAIL ⇒ batch blocked + rejected |
| `POST /qc/batches/:id/certificate` | Issue certificate (requires all-PASS) |
| `GET /qc/batches/:id/trace-back` | Failed batch → contributing samitis (root cause) |

## Traceability (`traceability.ts`) - public (§8.4)
| `GET /trace/:code` | QR → full provenance: product, batch, plant, samiti-level sources with volume shares (§7.4 honesty), tests, certificate |
| `GET /trace/codes` | Demo helper (mock only; optional in prod) |

## Cattle & 1962 (`cattle.ts`) - §9/§10
| `GET /animals?ownerPartyId` · `GET /animals/:id` | Cattle (Pashu Aadhaar as join key) |
| `POST /animals/:id/events` | Health/AI event (+ Bharat Pashudhan sync flag) |
| `POST /vet-requests` · `GET /vet-requests?requestedByPartyId` | 1962 MVU visit requests |

## Commerce (`commerce.ts`) - §11
| `GET /products` | Active catalogue |
| `POST /orders` · `GET /orders?consumerPartyId` · `GET /orders/:id` | Orders |

## Education & schemes (`education.ts`)
| `GET /education` | Vernacular content (offline-cached flags) |
| `GET /schemes?applicantPartyId` · `POST /schemes` | Nand Baba scheme applications (DBT status) |

## Admin (`admin.ts`) - §12
| `GET /admin/stats` | Control-tower aggregates |
| `GET /admin/parties?q` | Party + assignment search |
| `POST /admin/role-assignments` · `POST /admin/role-assignments/:id/revoke` | Org-scoped, time-bounded grants (§4.1); revoke = close validity window |
| `GET /admin/feature-flags` · `PUT /admin/feature-flags/:key` | Capability gating (collar dormant path, §3.6/§9) |
| `GET /admin/audit-events?limit` | Append-only audit trail |
| `GET /admin/products` · `PUT /admin/products` | Product master |

## Dashboards (`dashboards.ts`)
| `GET /dashboards/farmer/:partyId` | FarmerSummary (today/month/pending + 12-day trend) |
| `GET /dashboards/society/:dcsId` | SocietyStats |

### Backend must also own (not expressible in the mock)
Append-only provenance semantics (§7.3), real OTP + Aadhaar-vault KYC (§18-A),
payment-rail integration behind human authorisation (§18-B), audit-log
immutability + 180-day retention (CERT-In), org-scope enforcement server-side

# Saathi - backend integration guide

How the mobile app (`parag-saathi-fe`) talks to the Go backend
(`parag-saathi-be`). This is the authoritative map of **frontend action →
backend route**, the wire conventions, and the **gaps** the backend still
needs to close for full parity.

## Wire conventions (all endpoints)

| Concern | Contract |
| --- | --- |
| Base URL | `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` + `/api/v1` (e.g. `http://host:8080/api/v1`) |
| Success envelope | `{ "data": … , "meta"?: {limit,offset,total} }` - the client unwraps `data` |
| Error envelope | `{ "error": { "code", "message", "details"? } }` → `ApiError` |
| Auth | `Authorization: Bearer <access token>`; 401 → one silent refresh + retry, then sign-out |
| Field case | **snake_case** on the wire; the app maps to camelCase via each endpoint's `mapResponse`/`mapRequest` |
| IDs | Mongo **ObjectIDs** (24-hex strings) - opaque to the client |
| Dates / times | `YYYY-MM-DD` (IST) for dates; ISO-8601 for timestamps |
| Idempotency | Pours carry `client_event_id` for offline-sync replay safety |

The app talks to the backend by default (`EXPO_PUBLIC_API_MODE=http`). An
in-app **mock** backend (`=mock`) serves the same typed calls for offline dev
and the demo build - every endpoint below has a mock, so screens work with or
without the server.

## Module map (backend mounts under `/api/v1`)

| Backend module | Mount | Frontend endpoint file |
| --- | --- | --- |
| identity | `/auth`, `/parties`, `/kyc`, `/roles` | `auth.ts`, parts of `admin.ts` |
| orgs | `/orgs` | `org.ts` |
| collection | `/collection` (`/pours`, `/invoices`, `/rate-charts`, `/readings`) | `collections.ts`, `payments.ts` |
| logistics | `/logistics` (`/consignments`, `/trips`) | `logistics.ts`, lots in `collections.ts` |
| plant | `/plant` (`/bmc-lots`, `/batches`, `/product-lots`, `/qrs`) | `plant.ts` |
| quality | `/quality` (`/limits`, `/qc-results`) | `quality.ts` |
| settlement | `/settlements`, `/dbt` | `payments.ts`, `education.ts` |
| cattle | `/cattle` (`/animals`, `/mvu-cases`, `/education`) | `cattle.ts`, `education.ts` |
| platformops | `/admin`, `/audit`, `/support`, `/notifications` | `admin.ts` |
| publictrace | `/public` (`/qr/{code}`), `/trace/{type}/{id}` | `traceability.ts` |

`POST /logistics/trips/{tripID}/deliver`.

current codebase, section by section: **Conforms** (built + aligned), **Diverges**

primarily a field-app effort behind the existing endpoint seams.

# Saathi Wire Contract & Domain Alignment Report
## Frontend (`parag-saathi-fe`, TS) ⇄ Backend (`parag-saathi-be`, Go)

Analysis is read-only. "Wire name" = the snake_case key the FE's `mapRequest`/`mapResponse` actually reads/writes (from `src/core/api/endpoints/*.ts`); "backend json" = the Go struct `json:` tag in `internal/domain/*.go` and module `models.go`.

---

## 1. WIRE CONVENTIONS

| Concern | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Base URL** | `http://localhost:8080/api/v1` (env `EXPO_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL`; default in `client.ts:26`). Backend confirms `/api/v1` tree in `internal/httpapi/router.go:65`. | ✅ aligned |
| **Module mount prefixes** | Backend mounts each module *under* `/api/v1`: `/auth`, `/parties`, `/kyc`, `/orgs`, `/collection`, `/logistics`, `/plant`, `/quality`, `/settlements`, `/dbt`, `/cattle`, `/public`. | ✅ FE endpoints use these exact prefixes (`/collection/pours`, `/logistics/consignments`, `/plant/batches`, `/quality/qc-results`, `/settlements`, `/public/qr/…`). |
| **Success envelope** | `{"data": ..., "meta"?: ...}` — `httpx` `envelope{Data, Meta}`. FE unwraps `.data` (`client.ts:148`), tolerates bare payloads. | ✅ aligned |
| **Error envelope** | `{"error": {"code", "message", "details"?}}` — `httpx.AppError{Code, Message, Details}`. FE maps to `ApiError(status, code, message, details)` (`client.ts:137-146`). | ✅ aligned |
| **Error code style** | UPPER_SNAKE string codes. Backend generic codes: `UNAUTHORIZED`, `FORBIDDEN`, `NOT_FOUND`, `METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `INTERNAL`, plus per-case codes (`CONSENT_REQUIRED`, etc.). FE falls back to `HTTP_<status>` if `error.code` absent. | ✅ style aligned. ⚠️ FE invents many domain codes the backend may not emit yet (`IMPLAUSIBLE_READING`, `QC_GATE_BLOCKED`, `LOT_NOT_DISPATCHED`) — these live only in mock bodies for mock-only endpoints. |
| **Auth header** | `Authorization: Bearer <access token>` (`client.ts:126`). | ✅ aligned |
| **Token model** | SESSION token from `POST /auth/otp/verify`; ROLE-scoped token from `POST /auth/role/select`; rotating refresh via `POST /auth/refresh` `{refresh_token}` → `{access_token, refresh_token}`. | ✅ aligned (`identity/models.go` `authTokensResponse`, `refreshRequest`, `roleSelectResponse`) |
| **Refresh-on-401** | Single-flight: one refresh + one retry per 401, never for `/auth/*` paths, `clearTokens()` + `onUnauthorized()` on failure (`client.ts:154-205`). | ✅ |
| **snake_case ⇄ camelCase** | **Per-endpoint, in FE code.** Each endpoint declares `mapRequest` (camel→snake) and `mapResponse` (snake→camel). There is **no global auto-transform** — each wire field is hand-mapped, which is exactly where the silent mismatches in §3 hide. | ⚠️ fragile by design |
| **ID format** | Backend `_id` = Mongo `primitive.ObjectID` → serialized as 24-char hex string; all relations are ObjectID refs. FE treats every ID as an opaque string. Round-trips fine on reads. ⚠️ **Request risk:** backend request structs type IDs as `primitive.ObjectID`, so FE sending an empty/placeholder string (e.g. `org_unit_id:''` in `updateRateConfig`, `payments.ts:368`) will **fail ObjectID unmarshalling** (400), not be accepted. | ⚠️ |
| **Date/time** | Timestamps: Go `time.Time` → RFC3339/ISO-8601; FE consumes ISO strings and `.slice(0,10)`. Day-keys: `pour_date`/`invoice_date`/`date` are `"YYYY-MM-DD"` strings (IST settlement-day key, `DateKeyIST`). | ✅ aligned |
| **Idempotency** | `client_event_id` — device-minted unique string, offline-replay key. Backend `MilkPour.ClientEventID` (`bson/json:"client_event_id"`, unique index) + `CreatePourRequest.ClientEventID` + `PourResponse.IdempotentReplay`. FE mints `nextId('evt')` per attempt (`collections.ts:225`). ⚠️ FE mints a **fresh** id every attempt, so a retried pour is a **new** event, defeating the dedupe (only true offline-queue replays would reuse an id — the current UI path does not). | ⚠️ semantics |
| **Pour create response** | `{"pour": MilkPour, "idempotent_replay"?: bool}` — FE reads `raw.pour` (`collections.ts:236`). | ✅ aligned |

---

## 2. ROLE CODES

FE `ROLE_CODES` (`roles.ts`, 24 entries; comment says "23" but lists 24) vs backend `domain.AllRoles` (24 entries). **22 shared, 2 FE-only, 2 backend-only.**

| Role code | FE `roles.ts` | Backend `AllRoles` | Note |
|---|:--:|:--:|---|
| FARMER, SAMITI_SACHEEV, SAMITI_ADHYAKSH, MILK_TESTER, LRP, AI_TECH | ✅ | ✅ | match (incl. the unusual spelling `SACHEEV`, and `MILK_TESTER`) |
| VAN_RIDER, DELIVERY_RIDER, BMC_OPERATOR, UNION_FIELD_SUPERVISOR, UNION_PRESIDENT | ✅ | ✅ | match |
| PLANT_OPERATOR, PLANT_LAB_ANALYST, PCDF_ADMIN, MISSION_OFFICIAL, DISTRICT_VERIFIER | ✅ | ✅ | match |
| VETERINARIAN, MVU_DRIVER, SUPPORT_AGENT, STATE_AUDITOR, SUPER_ADMIN, SERVICE_ACCOUNT | ✅ | ✅ | match |
| **`ONBOARDING_EXECUTIVE`** | ✅ | ❌ | **MISMATCH.** Backend's equivalent is **`ORGANISING_MANAGER`**. FE cannot select this role against the real backend (role token issuance would reject an unknown code); a member holding it won't appear correctly. |
| **`STORE_MANAGER`** | ✅ | ❌ | **MISMATCH.** No backend role. The retail/store module is FE-only. |
| **`ORGANISING_MANAGER`** | ❌ | ✅ | **MISMATCH.** Backend's ground-level KYC/onboarding role. If the backend returns this in `/parties/me` assignments, FE `ROLES[code]` lookup is **`undefined`** → role switcher crash. |
| **`CONSUMER`** | ❌ | ✅ | **MISMATCH.** Backend has a `CONSUMER` role (KYC `MINIMAL`); FE has a consumer *app* but no `CONSUMER` role code → same `undefined` lookup risk. |

**KYC tier enum mismatch:** FE `KycTier` = `MINIMAL | FARMER | STANDARD | RIDER | HIGH | HIGHEST | **MTLS**`; backend tiers = `… | HIGHEST | **SERVICE**`. The service-account tier is **`MTLS` (FE)` vs `SERVICE` (backend)`** — mismatch.

---

## 3. ENTITY FIELD MAP + MISMATCHES

Legend: **🔴 silent-break** (wire names differ → field silently defaults to `0`/`''`/`[]`); **🟠 enum mismatch**; **🟡 FE-only / lossy**; ✅ aligned.

### Party  (`domain.Party`)
| FE domain | FE wire read | Backend json | |
|---|---|---|---|
| id / name / phone / kycTier / createdAt | id / full_name / phone / kyc_tier / created_at | id / full_name / phone / kyc_tier / created_at | ✅ |
| aadhaarMasked, bankVerified | from `kyc` summary: `aadhaar_last4`, `bank_verified` | `kycSummary.aadhaar_last4`, `bank_verified` | ✅ (⚠️ FE `WireKycSummary.tier` vs backend `requested_tier` — mismatch, but FE doesn't read `tier`, so benign) |
| **nameHi, village, publicConsent** | — | *(absent)* | 🟡 **FE-only.** `publicConsent` (§6.7 opt-in to be named on public trace) has **no backend Party field** — the consented-farmer trace can't be driven. |

### RoleAssignment  (`domain.RoleAssignment`)
| FE | wire | backend json | |
|---|---|---|---|
| id, partyId, role, orgUnitId, validFrom, validTo | id, party_id, role_code, org_unit_id, valid_from, valid_to | same | ✅ |
| active | `status === 'ACTIVE'` | status (`ACTIVE`/`REVOKED`) | ✅ |
| roster row (`/orgs/{id}/members`) | party_id, role_code, **role_assignment_id**, valid_from, valid_to | `orgs.Member` same | ✅ |

### OrgUnit  (`domain.OrgUnit`)
| FE | wire | backend json | |
|---|---|---|---|
| id, name, code | id, name, code | id, name, code | ✅ |
| **type** | org_type / type | type | 🟠 **enum:** FE `FEDERATION\|UNION\|DCS\|BMC\|PLANT\|STORE\|DISTRICT` vs backend `FEDERATION\|MILK_UNION\|PROCESSING_PLANT\|BMC\|DCS`. FE **`UNION`≠`MILK_UNION`**, FE **`PLANT`≠`PROCESSING_PLANT`**, FE `STORE`/`DISTRICT` have no backend type. `auth.ts` casts raw `org_type` straight to the FE union → invalid values leak through. |
| geo `{lat,lng}` | *(not mapped in auth.ts)* | flat `geo_lat`/`geo_lng` | 🔴 structure mismatch (nested vs flat); FE org mapper drops geo entirely. |
| nameHi, village | — | *(absent)* | 🟡 FE-only |

### Pour  (`domain.MilkPour`)  — POST `/collection/pours`

## 4. FE-DOMAIN CONCEPTS THE BACKEND DOMAIN LACKS

1. **`Pour.assurance` (A|B|C)** — capture-assurance level (§6.2). No backend field/enum; FE derives it client-side from entry method. Downstream `DcsLot.assurance` (weakest-of-set) also FE-only.
2. **`rate_chart_version` / `RateConfig.version` / `Pour.rateChartVersion`** — backend pins pricing via `rate_chart_id` (ObjectID ref), has no immutable version string.
3. **Tamper seal: `DcsLot.sealCode`/`sealedAt`, `RouteStop.sealCode`** (§6.4) — backend `DCSConsignment` and `RouteStop` have **no seal fields**; the van-rider seal-match check (`SEAL_MISMATCH`) is mock-only.
4. **`Party.publicConsent`** (§6.7 opt-in to public trace) — no backend Party field → consented-farmer names on the trace can't be sourced.
5. **`Animal.ageMonths`, `lactationNo`, `avgDailyYieldLitres`** — backend has only `birth_date` + `lactation_status`. (Neither side has the "tag_status" the brief asked about.)
6. **`OnboardingRequest` entity** (assisted-KYC, `onboarding.ts` + `domain.ts`) — no backend counterpart; backend models this as `KYCRecord` + `Party` + `RoleAssignment` (fundamentally different shape).
7. **`ConsignmentInvoice`** (DCS→Union B2B GST e-invoice, HSN 0401) — FE-only, mock-only; no backend entity.
8. **`ReleaseSummary` + assisted-release stage machine** (`PENDING_APPROVAL\|UNION_FUNDED\|DISTRIBUTING\|FARMERS_PAID`) — FE-only; backend `SettlementBatch` uses a different vocabulary (`INITIATED\|PENDING_APPROVAL\|APPROVED\|EXECUTING\|EXECUTED\|PARTIAL\|FAILED\|REJECTED`) with a `PayoutInstruction` sub-entity.
9. **Invoice gross/deductions/net model** — backend Invoice carries a single `total_amount`; no deductions concept.
10. **Batch-embedded `contributingDcsIds`, `productOutputs`, `certificateId`, `qcStatus`, `volumeLitres`** — none exist on `ProcessingBatch`; they're separate collections (`ProductLot`, `QCResult`) or absent.
11. **Retail/last-mile domain**: `Delivery`, `DeliveryPreferences`, `StoreInventoryItem`, `RiderSummary`, `Order`/`OrderItem`, `Product` catalogue — **no backend domain files** for store/commerce/delivery.
12. **`SchemeApplication`, `EducationContent` (FE shape), `FeatureFlag`, `AuditEvent` (FE shape), `HealthEvent.CHECKUP`** — partial/absent. Backend has `EducationContent` (different fields: `media_type`/`media_url`/`duration_sec`), platform `audit`, and routes subsidies via `DBTRequest` (not FE's `SchemeApplication`).

**Conversely, backend-only entities the FE has no model for:** `AnalyzerReading` (separate reading record with anti-tamper envelope), `KYCRecord`, `Consent`, `DocRef`, `SettlementBatch`, `PayoutInstruction`, `DBTRequest`, `Notification`, `ColdChainEntry`, and `ProvenanceSeq` on every ledgered entity.
